tagline.text: Mindanao's little Boracay, spread along Sarangani Bay

items.credit: Michael E. Peligro / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons
Michael E. Peligro / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: Gumasa in Glan, Sarangani, is a beach known as "Mindanao's little Boracay," with about 6km of fine white sand and jade-colored shallows. It's 1–2 hours by car from General Santos, and every year in late May it hosts Sarbay Fest, Mindanao's biggest beach festival.
Gumasa Beach is in Barangay Gumasa, Glan, on the eastern shore of Sarangani Bay at Mindanao's southern tip. Flour-fine white sand runs about
6km

along a series of bow-shaped coves, and at low tide, knee-deep jade shallows stretch out several hundred meters. The sand is packed firm enough that many visitors say walking barefoot feels like walking on a smooth floor, which is why locals have long called it "Mindanao's little Boracay."
The sea off the beach falls within the Sarangani Bay Protected Seascape, designated by Presidential Proclamation No. 756 in

. Covering about 210,000 hectares, it's one of the largest marine protected areas in the Philippines, safeguarding sea turtle nesting grounds, coral reefs, and the deep bay waters visited by whales and dolphins together. The water around the rocky points at each end of the beach is clear and good for snorkeling, and at sunset, the sun dropping behind the mountains across the bay bathes the beach in red.
Glan began as an agricultural colony (Colony No. 9) founded in

by settlers who arrived by boat from Cebu, and traces of the old wooden houses and early settlement days still remain in the town, which is now known as Sarangani's heritage town. Glan is also the town Sarangani promotes as its "tourism capital," with Gumasa Beach at its heart.

Unlike Boracay, it's not lined with shops and bars — just a handful of family resorts, shady palm trees, and a quiet sea. On weekends, Holy Week, and summer break, though, it fills up with families visiting from General Santos and the Cotabato area. It suits travelers who want to relax on an uncrowded white-sand beach, or anyone wanting to add a beach day to a General Santos business trip or tuna food tour.
Walk between the resorts along
6km
of white sand. Early in the morning, the water is calm and there are few people around, giving you the feeling of having the whole beach to yourself.

At low tide, clear knee-deep water stretches out far, making it good for playing in the water with kids. When the tide comes in, it quickly becomes deep enough to swim, so just check the tide times and enjoy accordingly.

The rocky areas at each end of the beach and in front of Isla Jardin del Mar Resort have clear water where you can see small coral and tropical fish. Bringing your own snorkel gear makes it much more convenient.
Since Gumasa sits on the bay's eastern shore, the sun sets over the mountains across the bay. Head out to the beach around
and you can capture the reddening sea and the silhouettes.
Held for about three days every
late May
, the Sarangani Bay Festival is Mindanao's biggest beach festival, featuring a color run, a skimboarding contest, sand sculpture, bangka races, a bay-crossing swim, and nightly performances.
Some resorts rent kayaks and paddleboards. A popular route is paddling along the coast in the morning, when winds are light, to explore the neighboring coves.
Glan town, about
10–15 minutes
from the beach by tricycle, still has wooden houses from the settlement era, an old town hall, and a plaza, making it a good short walking break between beach sessions.
Arrive at General Santos Airport, then taxi to the van terminal at KCC Mall
Board a van to Glan, then take a tricycle from the Glan terminal to your Gumasa resort
Check in and have lunch, then play in the shallows timed with low tide
Watch the Sarangani Bay sunset from the beach, then dinner of grilled tuna and kinilaw at the resort
Walk and photograph the empty beach early in the morning
Snorkel at the rocky points, or kayak and paddleboard
Check out, then walk among the heritage houses in Glan town
Take a van back to General Santos for a tuna dinner, or continue to your next destination
For 3 days and 2 nights, spending the whole second day resting on the beach and touring Glan town and the Burias-side beach on the third morning before heading back makes for a relaxed trip.
Philippine Airlines and Cebu Pacific fly daily direct from Manila to General Santos International Airport (GES), taking about
1 hour 50 minutes–2 hours
. One-way fares run around
depending on the season. Cebu also has direct flights, taking about
1 hour 20 minutes
. The airport is north of downtown, about
30–45 minutes
by taxi to KCC Mall downtown, for around
Vans to Glan leave from the terminal next to KCC Mall in General Santos once they fill up with passengers. The roughly
60km
route runs along Sarangani Bay through Alabel and Malapatan, taking about
1 hour–1 hour 30 minutes
, for around
. After getting off at the Glan town terminal, another
10–15 minutes
by tricycle reaches the Gumasa resort area, with fares around
depending on the number of passengers and the resort's location.
Coming from Davao, take a bus such as Yellow Bus Line from the Ecoland bus terminal (DCOTT) to General Santos, about
3–4 hours
, for around
. From General Santos, transfer to a van to Glan as described above.
For a family or group, renting a van with driver for the day in General Santos is convenient. Including the round trip and waiting time, it runs about
per van, and you can also head straight to Gumasa from the airport. The coastal road is well paved, but it's best to avoid traveling after dark.
You can walk between resorts along the beach. For Glan town and nearby beaches, use a tricycle or habal-habal (motorbike taxi); negotiate a half-day charter for around
. It's convenient to ask the resort front desk to arrange your return transport in advance.
December
through
May
is the best time to visit, with little rain and clear seas.
March–May
in particular has strong sun and the prettiest water, but daytime temperatures climb to
, and resorts and cottages book out early during Holy Week and Sarbay Fest in
late May
. To catch the festival, book your accommodation weeks ahead, and if you want a quiet beach, it's best to avoid festival week and Holy Week.
June
through
November

is the rainy season, with frequent afternoon showers and days when the water turns cloudy. Southern Mindanao sits outside the Philippines' main typhoon path, though, so direct typhoon hits are rare, and most days see a short downpour rather than rain all day. Weekdays keep resorts quiet and rates easy to negotiate, giving the off-season its own advantages.

Accommodation is essentially just the family-style resorts lined up along Gumasa Beach. Isla Jardin del Mar, an established resort accredited by the Department of Tourism, is the best known, with gardens, a walking path along the rocky point, and a snorkeling spot. Coco Beach, Rosal Beach, White Haven, and Crystal AC Beach Resort also sit side by side along the shore, with fan rooms running about
a night and air-conditioned beachfront rooms around
. Each resort charges its own day-use entrance fee and cottage rate separately, so factor that in if you're stopping by without staying overnight.

The food centers on Sarangani Bay seafood. Being close to General Santos, the Philippines' tuna capital, you can enjoy grilled tuna jaw (panga), tuna kinilaw (vinegar-cured sashimi), and tuna sinigang cheaply and fresh. There aren't many options beyond the resort restaurants, so a common local-style outing is buying fish, fruit, and drinks at the General Santos market or in Glan town and grilling them at your cottage. Most resorts rent out a charcoal grill.
Gumasa has no ATM, and most resorts take cash only. Withdraw plenty of cash in General Santos or Glan town before you come.
It's best to plan your water activities around the tide table. Low tide suits walking in the shallows, and high tide suits swimming and snorkeling.
During Holy Week, summer break, and Sarbay Fest weekends, cottages sell out by morning, so book the day before or arrive early.
The beach is public, but most access points run through resort property, so it's standard to pay an entrance fee no matter which resort you go through.
For sunset, the central resorts with an open view work better than the north end of the beach.
Vans departing Glan thin out significantly around sunset. It's safest to leave the beach by
3–4 PM
at the latest.
Smart and Globe data signal is weak or drops out in some spots, so it's best to take care of any calls you need in Glan town beforehand.
The rocky points have sea urchins and sharp coral, so aqua shoes make things much easier.

Travel advisories from various governments recommend against non-essential travel to most of Mindanao, with a few exceptions such as Davao City and Cagayan de Oro City, and Sarangani falls within that area. Check your home country's latest travel advisory before you go, and if you do visit, travel only on main roads during daylight hours.
Southern Mindanao is an area where armed group activity and kidnapping risks have been reported. Check local news and embassy notices, and let your accommodation and someone you know know your route.
Most of the beach has no lifeguard on duty. Some spots get suddenly deep at high tide, so children and weak swimmers should wear a life vest.

Sarangani Bay is a protected seascape, so collecting coral or shells and touching sea turtles are prohibited. Rules can change based on notices from the protected area management board, so check the latest updates.
Midday UV exposure is very strong, causing frequent sunburn and dehydration. Book a shaded cottage and bring plenty of water.
Jellyfish appear at certain times of year, so wear a rash guard, and rinse with vinegar if stung.
About
1 hour–1 hour 30 minutes
from Gumasa by car, the tuna capital, famous for its dawn fish port auction and tuna dishes.
A crater lake in the T'boli highlands, reached by about
3–4 hours
by car via General Santos, followed by a trek.
